# Cross Validation {#sec-cross-validation}

<!-- Simplified from the 2025 STAT 8670 Cross Validation lecture. All figures are generated below. -->

```{r}
#| label: cv-setup
#| include: false
#| cache: false
library(ggplot2)
cv_ink <- "#51464C"
cv_rose <- "#C86C85"
cv_mint <- "#5B9682"
cv_lavender <- "#8B80B9"
cv_cream <- "#FFF9F2"
cv_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 12, base_family = "sans") +
  theme(
```

Monte Carlo simulation generates inputs from a specified model. **Cross-validation (CV)** reuses observed data to ask a different question: **how well will a fitting method predict new observations?** We use CV to compare models and choose their complexity.

The main idea is **fit on one part, predict the part left out, and average the prediction errors**. We use one polynomial regression example throughout.

## Prediction on New Observations {#sec-cv-prediction}

For regression, we want the **average squared prediction error on independent new observations** from the same population.

**Training error** uses the observations that fitted the model. It is usually optimistic: the model has already used their outcomes to choose its coefficients. To assess prediction, evaluate observations left out of fitting.

For $m$ held-out observations, calculate

$$
\operatorname{MSE}=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2.
$$

For classification, we could instead average $\mathbf{1}\{y_i\ne\widehat y_i\}$ to estimate the misclassification rate. Choose the loss before comparing models.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv-data-roles
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-cap: "Training fits the coefficients; validation chooses the model; a separate test set assesses the chosen procedure. CV rotates the training and validation roles within the development data."
#| fig-alt: "A mint training card and pink validation card sit inside development data. A separate lavender test card is used after model selection."
grid::grid.newpage()
grid::grid.rect(gp = grid::gpar(fill = cv_cream, col = NA))
grid::grid.roundrect(.34, .46, .61, .73, r = grid::unit(4, "mm"),
  gp = grid::gpar(fill = "#F2EEE8", col = "#DACBC6", lwd = 1.2))
grid::grid.text("Development data", .34, .77,
  gp = grid::gpar(col = cv_ink, fontsize = 15, fontface = "bold"))
cv_card <- function(x, title, body, fill) {
  grid::grid.roundrect(x, .43, .255, .45, r = grid::unit(4, "mm"),
    gp = grid::gpar(fill = fill, col = NA))
  grid::grid.text(title, x, .53,
    gp = grid::gpar(col = cv_ink, fontsize = 14, fontface = "bold"))
  grid::grid.text(body, x, .36,
    gp = grid::gpar(col = cv_ink, fontsize = 12, lineheight = 1.2))
}
cv_card(.19, "Train", "Fit\ncoefficients", "#D8EBE1")
cv_card(.49, "Validate", "Compare\ncandidates", "#F6D8DF")
cv_card(.83, "Test", "Assess once\nafter selection", "#E6DFF2")
grid::grid.text("CV rotates these roles", .34, .145,
  gp = grid::gpar(col = cv_ink, fontsize = 11))
grid::grid.lines(c(.66, .69), c(.43, .43),

```

A single training/validation split is simple, but its result depends on which observations were held out. CV spreads validation across several subsets. A final **test set** remains separate from this model-selection process.

## One Example: Choose a Polynomial Degree {#sec-cv-example}

We compare polynomial regressions

$$
\widehat f_d(x)=\widehat\beta_0+\widehat\beta_1x+\cdots+\widehat\beta_dx^d,
\qquad d\in\{1,\ldots,8\}.
$$

The degree $d$ is a **hyperparameter**: it specifies the model's flexibility. The coefficients $\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_d$ are **parameters** estimated from training data after we fix $d$. **Hyperparameter tuning** compares candidate settings using validation error. Here least squares estimates the coefficients; CV chooses the degree.

Other hyperparameters include the ridge penalty $\lambda$ and the number of neighbors in $k$-nearest neighbors. The number of CV folds $K$ controls the **evaluation procedure**, not the polynomial's flexibility.

Generate one illustrative data set with a quadratic mean and random noise. Reserve 40 observations for the final test; use 80 for development. All observations are generated independently, so these disjoint groups are independent samples.

```{r}
#| label: cv-example-data
#| code-fold: false
set.seed(8670)
x <- runif(120, -2, 2)
dat <- data.frame(x, y = 1 + 2 * x - x^2 + rnorm(120, sd = 0.7))
development <- dat[1:80, ]
test <- dat[81:120, ]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv-model-flexibility
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Degree 1 underfits the curved pattern. Degree 2 follows it well. Degree 8 has more freedom to fit noise; held-out error tells us whether that flexibility helps. The dashed curve is the known simulation mean, not information available to CV."
#| fig-alt: "Three panels show degree 1 missing the curvature, degree 2 following the quadratic mean, and degree 8 adding flexibility. All show the same observations and the true mean."
cv_grid <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 301))
cv_panels <- c("Degree 1: underfit", "Degree 2: good fit", "Degree 8: more flexible")
cv_fit_curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(cv_panels), function(j) {
  d <- c(1, 2, 8)[j]
  fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, d), data = development)
  data.frame(x = cv_grid$x, y = predict(fit, cv_grid), Panel = cv_panels[j])
}))
cv_fit_curves$Panel <- factor(cv_fit_curves$Panel, levels = cv_panels)
cv_truth <- data.frame(x = cv_grid$x, y = 1 + 2 * cv_grid$x - cv_grid$x^2)
cv_draw(ggplot(development, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "#F2CBD3", color = "#A66B7E", size = 1.9, alpha = .75) +
  geom_line(data = cv_truth, linetype = "dashed", color = "#766D70", linewidth = .6) +
  geom_line(data = cv_fit_curves, aes(color = Panel), linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~Panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(cv_lavender, cv_mint, cv_rose)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-2, 0, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Input x", y = "Response y", title = "More flexibility changes the fitted curve") +
  guides(color = "none"))
```

### Underfitting and Overfitting

**Underfitting:** the model is too restrictive to capture the main pattern. A straight line misses the curvature here. Training and validation errors tend to be large relative to a suitable model. Increasing flexibility can help.

**Overfitting:** the model adapts to training-sample noise that does not generalize. A typical sign is training error falling while validation error increases. A high degree creates the possibility of overfitting; complexity alone does not prove it.

A rigid model can have high **bias** (systematically miss the mean pattern). A flexible model can have high **variance** (change substantially with another training sample). We want enough flexibility to learn the pattern without fitting too much noise.

For nested least-squares models, training MSE cannot increase when we add polynomial terms. **Choosing by training MSE therefore favors the largest degree, even when prediction gets worse.** CV compares held-out errors instead; see the error curves below.

## How K-Fold CV Works {#sec-cv-kfold}

Split the $n$ development observations into $K$ roughly equal **folds**. Each fold serves once as validation data; the other $K-1$ folds supply the training data. Every observation receives a prediction from a model fitted **without that observation**.

For one fixed degree, 5-fold CV means **five separate fits**. Keep the degree fixed but estimate new coefficients each time. Each observation is used for validation once and training four times; it never serves both roles in the same fit.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv-folds
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-cap: "In 5-fold CV, each row is a fresh model fit. Pink is held out; mint is used for training. With 80 observations, each fit trains on 64 and predicts the remaining 16."
#| fig-alt: "A five-by-five grid has pink validation cells on the diagonal and mint training cells elsewhere, showing the held-out fold rotating across five fits."
cv_tiles <- expand.grid(Fold = 1:5, Fit = 1:5)
cv_tiles$Role <- ifelse(cv_tiles$Fold == cv_tiles$Fit, "Validate", "Train")
cv_draw(ggplot(cv_tiles, aes(Fold, Fit)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = Role), width = .91, height = .78, color = "#FFFEFC", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Role), size = 3.8, color = cv_ink, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Train = "#CDE5D9", Validate = "#F3C5D1")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5, labels = paste("Fold", 1:5), position = "top", expand = expansion(.02)) +
  scale_y_reverse(breaks = 1:5, labels = paste("Fit", 1:5), expand = expansion(.04)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Held-out folds rotate across fits") +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(color = cv_ink)))
```

::: {.callout-algorithm title="K-fold CV for model comparison"}

1. Choose the candidate models and the loss. Randomly assign the development observations to $K$ folds; use the **same folds for every candidate**.
2. For each candidate, and for each fold $k$, fit a fresh model on all folds except $k$.
3. Predict the outcomes in fold $k$ and store their losses. Repeat until every observation has one held-out prediction.
4. Average all $n$ held-out losses to obtain that candidate's CV error. Select the candidate with the smallest error.

:::

Let $S_k$ contain the indices in fold $k$, and let $\widehat f_d^{(-k)}$ be the degree-$d$ model fitted without that fold. Then

$$
\operatorname{CV}(d)
=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in S_k}
\left(y_i-\widehat f_d^{(-k)}(x_i)\right)^2.
$$

**What is averaged?** The squared errors of the held-out predictions. If a held-out outcome is 3 and its prediction is 2.5, it contributes $(3-2.5)^2=0.25$. With $n=80$, sum all 80 such errors and divide by 80. Equal-sized folds also allow averaging their MSEs; unequal folds require weights $|S_k|/n$.

## Leave-One-Out CV (LOOCV) {#sec-cv-loocv}

LOOCV is **$K=n$**: each validation fold contains one observation. For a fixed degree $d$, our 80 development observations give:

| Fit | Training observations | Held-out prediction |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | All except observation 1 | Predict $y_1$ from $x_1$ |
| 2 | All except observation 2 | Predict $y_2$ from $x_2$ |
| $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ |
| 80 | All except observation 80 | Predict $y_{80}$ from $x_{80}$ |

Write $\widehat f_d^{(-i)}$ for the model **refitted without observation $i$**. Average its $n$ held-out squared errors:

$$
\operatorname{CV}_{\mathrm{LOO}}(d)
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(y_i-\widehat f_d^{(-i)}(x_i)\right)^2.
$$

Each fit supplies **one squared error**, not a useful error estimate by itself. Predicting all observations with a model fitted to all $n$ would give training error, not LOOCV. Repeat the leave-one-out procedure for each candidate degree.

LOOCV trains on almost all the data but usually costs more: 80 fits per degree here, versus 5 for 5-fold CV. For a deterministic fitting method, LOOCV has no random fold assignment. Its score still varies across new data sets; it is not automatically more accurate or less variable than 5-fold CV.

## Select, Refit, and Test {#sec-cv-select}

Now **tune $d$ using 5-fold CV**: the outer loop tries degrees $1,\ldots,8$; the inner loop computes a CV score for one fixed degree. Choose

$$
d^*=\arg\min_{d\in\{1,\ldots,8\}}\operatorname{CV}(d).
$$

`prediction[fold == k]` stores the held-out predictions. `poly(x, d)` uses a numerically stable basis for a degree-$d$ polynomial.

```{r}
#| label: cv-comparison-code
#| code-fold: false
K <- 5
fold <- sample(rep(1:K, length.out = nrow(development)))
degrees <- 1:8
cv_mse <- numeric(length(degrees))
for (d in degrees) {
  prediction <- numeric(nrow(development))
  for (k in 1:K) {
    fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, d), data = development[fold != k, ])
    prediction[fold == k] <- predict(fit, development[fold == k, ])
  }
  cv_mse[d] <- mean((development$y - prediction)^2)
}
best_degree <- degrees[which.min(cv_mse)]
```

```{r}
#| label: cv-training-scores
#| include: false
cv_train_mse <- vapply(degrees, function(d) {
  mean(residuals(lm(y ~ poly(x, d), data = development))^2)
}, numeric(1))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv-error-curves
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Training error keeps falling, while CV reaches its minimum at degree 2. The right panel enlarges degrees 2-8; its vertical scale differs from the left panel. Both curves use the same development data; only CV predictions exclude the scored observations."
#| fig-alt: "Training and CV errors are plotted against polynomial degree. CV is smallest at degree 2; a second panel shows the small increases in CV for more flexible models."
cv_scores <- rbind(
  data.frame(Degree = degrees, MSE = cv_train_mse, Error = "Training"),
  data.frame(Degree = degrees, MSE = cv_mse, Error = "Cross-validation"))
cv_score_panels <- rbind(transform(cv_scores, View = "All candidates"),
  transform(subset(cv_scores, Degree >= 2), View = "Closer view: degrees 2-8"))
cv_score_panels$View <- factor(cv_score_panels$View,
  levels = c("All candidates", "Closer view: degrees 2-8"))
cv_draw(ggplot(cv_score_panels, aes(Degree, MSE, color = Error, shape = Error, linetype = Error)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) + geom_point(size = 2.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_degree, linetype = "dotted", color = "#9A8A90", linewidth = .6) +
  facet_wrap(~View, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Cross-validation" = cv_rose, Training = cv_mint)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Cross-validation" = 16, Training = 17)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Cross-validation" = "solid", Training = "dashed")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "Polynomial degree", y = "Mean squared error", title = "Choose by held-out error"))
```

CV selects degree **`r best_degree`**, with MSE **`r sprintf("%.3f", min(cv_mse))`**. We now refit that degree on **all 80 development observations**, then use the 40 reserved test observations once:

```{r}
#| label: cv-final-fit
#| code-fold: false
final_fit <- lm(y ~ poly(x, best_degree), data = development)
test_prediction <- predict(final_fit, newdata = test)
c(degree = best_degree, test_MSE = mean((test$y - test_prediction)^2))
```

The final model is a **new fit on all development data**, not the best-scoring fold's model. We use $8\times5=40$ CV fits and one final fit. We average held-out losses to choose the degree, not the five fitted models.

The test MSE estimates prediction error for this final fit. It need not equal the CV MSE: CV used smaller training sets and different held-out observations. The minimum CV error can also be optimistic because we selected it from several candidates. **If test error makes us change the degree, that set has become another validation set.** Keep it out of model selection.

## Choose Folds and Avoid Leakage {#sec-cv-choices}

**5-fold or 10-fold CV** is a useful starting point for independent observations. Each fit uses a fraction $(K-1)/K$ of the development data: with $n=80$, that means 64 training observations for 5-fold, 72 for 10-fold, and 79 for LOOCV.

Larger $K$ reduces the training-size difference from the final fit but requires more fits. This training-size issue is different from model bias due to underfitting. Increasing $K$ does not automatically improve the model or make CV less variable. A repeated-CV illustration is in [Supplementary](#sec-cv-supplement).

Two practical details determine whether the comparison is fair:

- **Fit the whole procedure inside each training fold.** Learn imputation, scaling, or feature selection using that fold's training observations, then apply those choices to its validation observations. Using validation outcomes to select features before CV leaks information.
- **Split according to the prediction task.** Keep repeated observations from the same person together when predicting new people. For future prediction, train on the past and validate on later times; randomly shuffling time points can use future information.

## Summary {#sec-cv-summary}

Cross-validation estimates how a **fitting procedure predicts observations excluded from training**. It helps choose a model or hyperparameter when the population prediction error cannot be calculated directly. Its score measures predictive performance for the chosen loss and a comparable population; it does not establish that the model is the true data-generating mechanism.

The workflow is: **define the prediction task and loss, hold out a test set, compare candidates by CV, refit the selected candidate, and assess it on the test set**. Use the same folds for all candidates, and keep all data-dependent fitting inside the training folds.

| Method | Training / validation per fit | Fits per candidate | Main consideration |
|:----------------|:--------------------------|:-----------------:|:-------------------------|
| One split | One training set / one holdout | 1 | Fast; sensitive to the split |
| $K$-fold CV | $K-1$ folds / one fold | $K$ | Every observation is held out once |
| LOOCV | $n-1$ observations / one | $n$ | Nearly full training size; often costly |
| Repeated $K$-fold (optional) | Repeat the fold assignment | $RK$ | Checks sensitivity to partitioning |

Here $n$ is the development sample size and $R$ is the number of repetitions. The separate final test set is not one of the CV folds.

### Repeated CV (optional)

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv-repeat-splits
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "Ten new 5-fold partitions of the same development data give slightly different CV curves. Only degrees 2-8 are shown to make nearby candidates visible. Thin curves are individual partitions; the thick curve is their average. No test observations are used."
#| fig-alt: "Ten pastel CV curves over degrees 2 through 8 show variation from reassigning folds, with a darker average curve and low errors near degree 2."
cv_repeat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = 10, ncol = length(degrees))
for (r in 1:10) {
  fold_r <- sample(rep(1:K, length.out = nrow(development)))
  for (d in degrees) {
    pred_r <- numeric(nrow(development))
    for (k in 1:K) {
      fit_r <- lm(y ~ poly(x, d), data = development[fold_r != k, ])
      pred_r[fold_r == k] <- predict(fit_r, development[fold_r == k, ])
    }
    cv_repeat[r, d] <- mean((development$y - pred_r)^2)
  }
}
cv_rep_long <- data.frame(Partition = rep(1:10, each = 8),
  Degree = rep(degrees, times = 10), MSE = as.vector(t(cv_repeat)))
cv_rep_mean <- data.frame(Degree = degrees, MSE = colMeans(cv_repeat))
cv_draw(ggplot(subset(cv_rep_long, Degree >= 2), aes(Degree, MSE)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Partition), color = "#D8AEC9", linewidth = .65, alpha = .75) +
  geom_point(aes(group = Partition), color = "#D8AEC9", size = 1.3, alpha = .75) +
  geom_line(data = subset(cv_rep_mean, Degree >= 2), color = cv_lavender, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = subset(cv_rep_mean, Degree >= 2), shape = 21, fill = "#E6DFF2",
    color = cv_lavender, size = 2.6, stroke = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:8) +
  labs(x = "Polynomial degree", y = "5-fold CV MSE", title = "A different split can change the comparison"))
```

Repeating CV checks sensitivity to the fold assignment; it does not create new observations. Here several degrees have similar scores. A tiny improvement in one partition is weak evidence for a more complex model. The repeated curves describe **split sensitivity**, not independent experiments or a confidence interval.
